A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MAD-based LLM evaluation study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained content across substantial rewriting and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original human evaluations of eight LLMs across four tasks, sampling comparisons, ablations, and model failure cases.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds automated-judge experiments, expanded model comparisons, and evaluations on MATH500 and Chatbot Arena Conversations.

M1.justification: The core discrepancy/diversity sampler remains intact. Appendix E.1 introduces an evaluated GPT-4o judge variant replacing human judgments, beyond v1's suggested future collaboration with LLM judges. Algorithm 2 also changes its stated Elo procedure from reaggregating combined comparisons to updating from existing ratings.

E1.justification: Section 4.6 adds evaluation on MATH500 and real dialogues from Chatbot Arena Conversations, extending validation beyond the synthesized instruction pools. The original four tasks and their seed datasets remain represented in Appendix B.

E2.justification: Anchor Points and DiffUse join random, KL-divergence, and cross-entropy sampling in the reasoning comparison: v1 Table 4 becomes v2 Table 2. Both additions also participate in the new writing-ranking comparison in v2 Table 8, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: New protocols include GPT-4o judging for the 20-model extension, 15-model MATH500 evaluation, and selecting 1,050 comparisons from a 15K Arena subset. Appendix E.2 specifies 630 instructions for DiffUse versus 210 for other seven-model samplers. The original eight-model inference settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds human-versus-GPT-4o ranking agreement, a five-value diversity-weight sweep, and validation addressing scalability and generalization beyond synthesized instructions. Existing metric and sample-size sensitivity analyses and failure cases remain. However, v1 Figure 6's per-model writing-length distributions are removed.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports inter-annotator agreement of 83.39%, correlation p-values, and three seeded random-sampling trials with a mean and standard deviation. Both versions already use 1,000 bootstrap samples for Elo aggregation; this is not an increased bootstrap count.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 scores and matched semantic-metric ablation scores remain unchanged. v2 adds substantial results for new samplers, writing comparisons, automated judging, 20 models, MATH500, and Arena subsets. Reported correlations include 0.993 on MATH500 and 0.986 for MAD's Arena subset. The removed writing histograms also remove several model-specific length summaries.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1's erroneous N(N−1)K response-pair count and formalizes the unordered-pair response set in Eq. (3), consistent with the existing algorithm. The similarity-to-discrepancy reformulation and rewritten Elo equations otherwise preserve the mathematics. No new proofs or theoretical guarantees appear.

C1.justification: The abstract strengthens the ranking-fidelity claim from obtaining a reliable, sensible ranking to recovering 'gold-standard' rankings with a handful of instructions. The central contributions—adaptive sampling, multidimensional evaluation, and diagnostic counterexamples—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning exhaustive-search cost and variable human cognitive load, alongside the retained annotation-scaling limitation. It also adds explanations of diversity-weight tradeoffs, baseline weaknesses, and when LLM judges can substitute for humans, while acknowledging distribution differences in leaderboard comparisons.

D1.justification: New documentation includes task-specific judge prompts, the GPT-4o judge version, baseline clustering and sampling configurations, and annotation redundancy, majority voting, workload, and duration. Existing hardware, inference parameters, evolution prompts, and code link largely remain. v1's explicit response-order shuffling for GPT-4 similarity assessment is no longer documented.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates its evaluation literature and positioning, adding Anchor Points, DiffUse, Prometheus, SaMer, J1, and newer benchmark references. It also removes several computational-vision and software-testing precedents cited in v1, including Ma et al. (2018) and Mckeeman (1998).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, results discussion, and appendices undergo extensive rewriting. Numbered method subsections replace paragraph headings, Algorithm 2 moves into the main text, and the appendices are reorganized around implementation, human evaluation, and additional results.

P2.justification: v2 redraws and relocates the pipeline, replaces the leaderboard table with a Sankey diagram, expands comparison tables, and adds experimental and judge-prompt tables. It relocates existing displays and removes the writing-length histograms. The redrawn sample-size plot labels its axis 0–8 despite retaining a 1–9 caption.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, external validation, broader baselines, and explicit limitations offer important potential gains. However, new Table 2 ranks contradict their Elo scores: Anchor Points places ChatGLM3-6B seventh at 1,023 but WizardLM-13B fourth at 877. Appendix D.4 also specifies at least five judgments for 1,120 pairs while reporting only about 345 pairs per each of 13 annotators. These unresolved inconsistencies affect the added accuracy and annotation-cost evidence, preventing a confident judgment of overall improvement.
